title: Interrupts
body:
[[Interrupt Driven I-O]]

An interrupt is a hardware-forced detour in the [[Fetch-Execute Cycle]]. A device raises a
signal, the [[CPU]] finishes the current instruction, saves its state, and jumps to a
handler instead of the next instruction. When the handler returns, the interrupted program
carries on with no idea it was ever paused.

The mechanism, in order:

1. Device asserts an [[IRQs|IRQ]]
2. The [[PIC]] ranks the pending requests with a [[Priority Encoder]] and presents the
   winning [[IPL]]
3. The CPU compares that level against the [[Interrupt Mask]]; if it does not win, it stays
   pending
4. The CPU pushes the PC and [[Status Register]], switches to [[Supervisor State]], and
   indexes the [[Vector Tables|vector table]]
5. The [[ISRs|ISR]] runs, saving and restoring whatever else it touches
   ([[Context Switching]])
6. `rte` restores the status register and the program resumes

Interrupts replace the busy wait of [[Polling]]: instead of the CPU asking "are you ready
yet", the device says so. The price is [[Concurrency]], because a handler can run between
any two instructions of the main program.

Terminology worth keeping straight: an *interrupt* is asynchronous and comes from outside
(a device); an *exception* or *trap* is synchronous and caused by the instruction being
executed (divide by zero, a [[System Call]]). The 68000 dispatches both through the same
vector table.
